controls.note: Untrusted prose uses text nodes; JSON responses are serialized, headers use fixed categories. Trusted authored build HTML has a separate parser/CSP boundary. The Chessground 10.4.2 adaptation moves one fixed SVG style declaration into trusted CSS with exact-version/fragment build guards, preserving style-src-attr denial; no untrusted text is added.
Library sources accept HTTP(S) URLs without credentials; record IDs are encoded and chess links use checked positions. External navigation privacy is assessed separately.
API/library messages use JSON serialization rather than concatenating untrusted JavaScript. Imported data is not emitted as executable source.
Usage and library values use bound SQLite parameters. Fixed migration/schema SQL is application-owned; no client-selected SQL is accepted.
The runtime exposes no OS-command tool or client-controlled process invocation. Chess tools run fixed browser engine operations; operator build commands are trusted development actions.
No WYSIWYG or untrusted HTML rendering feature exists. PGN/model/library text is treated as text. parse5 parses trusted authored build input; it is not used as an untrusted HTML sanitizer.
No application path evaluates model, PGN or user text as JavaScript. Workers and WASM load trusted build/catalogue assets; tools use a fixed allowlist. This does not certify third-party internals.
No XML parser or user XML input exists. The shipped SVG icon is a trusted static asset.
The validation guide records expected structures, limits, browser/server responsibilities and references to authoritative source constants and tests.
Gateway roles/provider/consent/limits and server library IDs, revisions, PGN and source metadata are checked before security-relevant work.
The Node gateway enforces its own message/privacy/admission checks; library writes independently validate shared record rules and recompile PGN. Browser checks alone do not authorize writes.

Library mutations use current-owner revisions and transactions. Provider routing/consent is captured after body reads; stale browser work is rejected by session/position checks. No financial or account workflow exists.
Static/API responses have explicit types, nosniff and frame isolation. Public paths reject hidden/private data; API JSON is not served as HTML. SVG charset remains a separate open item.
Coach, imports and literal highlights use text nodes rather than HTML interpolation. Browser regressions exercise hostile markup and regex-like text.

Protected HTTPS usage/library cookies have __Secure- names, Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict and separate canonical API paths without Domain. Standard native/image launches require supplied TLS before opening storage; API constructors refuse plaintext by default. Existing valid legacy IDs migrate unchanged, preserving usage hashes/library owner keys, revisions and schema; ambiguous or malformed secure identities fail without cookie replacement. Browser/profile rollback and the actual previous HTTPS CLI retain post-upgrade writes/counters. Explicit HTTP development uses separate kibitz_dev_* identities and cannot adopt production cookies. This verifies cookie protection for the supported TLS mode, not authentication, HSTS, endpoint/public-cert evidence or default-branch alert dismissal. See the scoped migration record; the other eleven final-release fixes remain open.

The local server intentionally has no HSTS policy and supports HTTP. A one-year localhost-wide policy would affect other apps and ports. Reassess transport and deployment before enabling it. Owner approved this documented local 0.1.0-rc.1 deviation on 2026-10-25, with review due 2026-11-01 and before another release or deployment/provider/runtime-scope change; the requirement remains unsatisfied. Owner direction requires this condition fixed and verified before the first final (non-prerelease) release; RC acceptance does not close the remediation TODO or extend the existing dates.
The server does not emit Access-Control-Allow-Origin or reflect arbitrary origins. No wildcard-sensitive CORS response is enabled.
Sensitive writes require JSON and provider consent headers where applicable; library access additionally checks fetch metadata and full native Origin. Direct local non-browser clients remain trusted.

All AI write routes require JSON and a full Origin matching the native socket scheme/host. Wrong HTTP/HTTPS, FTP, blob and null Origins are rejected despite forwarding-header spoofing. Direct local clients without Origin remain trusted; preflight receives no CORS approval.

Provider work/configuration and library writes/erase require POST/DELETE as appropriate. GET status/read paths do not perform inference or mutate private records; minting a grouping cookie is not authentication.

JSON, NDJSON, HTML, JS, CSS, text and SVG responses declare UTF-8 with their corresponding media type. Actual CLI GET/HEAD and browser SVG document checks verify the former SVG gap; binary/unknown assets remain binary media types.
There is no WebSocket service/client. Coaching uses HTTP NDJSON, and in-page workers use local message channels.

There is no arbitrary file-upload endpoint. Pasted PGN/JSON is bounded separately. The operator model downloader enforces catalogue size, streaming byte limits and a total deadline before publication.

Model downloads use fixed GGUF catalogue names and verify exact length/hash before publication; cached files are scoped to the operator-controlled model directory. PGN content is parsed as chess data, not accepted by extension alone.

The static server reads descriptors as bytes and does not execute uploaded/generated data as Node code. Private library/usage files stay outside the static tree; catalogue model serving is narrowly scoped.

Static/model/private file boundaries reject traversal, hidden paths and symlink substitution; model filenames and fixture output names come from fixed allowlists. This is scoped to the implemented entry points.
No application sign-in or password verification exists, so no credential-stuffing/lockout policy is claimed. Usage admission is not authentication protection.
The application has no user password creation or validation. Server provider API keys are operator credentials, not account passwords.
There is no application password or password-change workflow.
There is no current/new application password transaction to authorize.
There is no password enrolment/reset input or password verifier to check against a denylist.
There is no user password policy or password field.
No application account password input exists. Provider secrets are configured server-side rather than entered into a browser account form.
No application password entry workflow exists to restrict paste or password managers.
There is no received account password that the application normalizes or verifies.
No credential authentication endpoint exists; local rate/token admission does not constitute brute-force protection for hosted accounts.
The app creates no root/admin/default user account or account registry. Local grouping cookies are not account authentication.
No account activation codes or initial passwords are generated. Random grouping cookies have a separate scoped assessment.
No password hints or security-question authentication feature exists.

New usage/library group identifiers are generated dynamically by the server rather than using static provider credentials. This verifies the token-generation property only, not authenticated sessions.
Usage identifiers use 16 random bytes and library identifiers 32 random bytes from Node crypto.randomBytes, encoded base64url. The full local identity/lifecycle limitations remain deviations.
There is no sign-in or reauthentication event. Grouping cookies do not establish authenticated sessions.

Server queries use the current opaque library cookie owner; record IDs alone do not grant another group access. API tests cover independent clients, ownership and revisions. This proves cookie isolation, not person authentication.

Node enforces current-owner library scope, revision and write rules without trusting browser owner fields. A locally trusted direct client remains inside the declared boundary; hosted authorization is absent.
No self-contained authorization token is accepted. Grouping cookies are opaque references, not JWT claims.
No self-contained token creation/verification or client-selected token algorithm exists.
No JWT issuer, token-key URL or self-contained-token key resolution is implemented.
No self-contained token claims or nbf/exp fields are parsed; grouping-cookie lifecycle deviations are tracked separately.
Kibitz is not an OAuth/OIDC authorization server and has no authorization redirect endpoint.
There is no OAuth authorization-code issue/redemption operation.
No OAuth authorization codes are generated or accepted.
No OAuth grants are configured or processed. Server provider API authentication is not an application OAuth authorization server.
No OAuth refresh tokens, refresh endpoint or authorization grant state exists.
The application does not implement bulk/asymmetric encryption or select padding modes. Node/browser transport TLS is assessed separately; persisted local data is not encrypted by the app.
There is no application-managed encryption cipher suite to approve. This is not a claim about provider infrastructure or a guarantee of encryption at rest.
Reviewed application integrity/scope digests use SHA-256 or HMAC-SHA-256; token entropy uses Node CSPRNG. Non-security retrieval signatures are not represented as cryptographic integrity.
